<!-- head-1: body_md -->
The space $\mathrm{Sp}_2$ of all $2\times2$ spin model subfactors, equipped with the metric $\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{MT}}$, is homeomorphic to the circle group $\mathbb{T}$:
\[
(\mathrm{Sp}_2,\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{MT}})\cong \mathbb{T}.
\]
In particular, $(\mathrm{Sp}_2,\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{MT}})$ is a compact and path connected metric space.
\vspace{0.2cm}
<!-- end head-1 -->
<!-- head-2: body_md -->
For any distinct $\alpha,\beta\in[0,\pi)$, we have
\[
\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{MT}}(\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\alpha},\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\beta})
= \left|\sin(\alpha-\beta)\right|.
\]
An immediate consequence of this explicit formula is that the distance between such spin model subfactors is not quantized; rather, every value in $[0,1]$ occurs as the Mashood--Taylor distance between some pair in this family (see Corollary \ref{cor:dmt-is-continuous}).
<!-- end head-2 -->
<!-- head-3: body_md -->
Let $\alpha,\beta\in[0,\pi)$ be distinct. Then the following quadruple
    \[
\begin{array}{ccc}
\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\alpha}  & \subset & \mathscr{R} \\
\cup && \cup \\
\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\alpha} \cap \mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\beta} & \subset & \mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\beta}
\end{array}
\]
is a commuting square if and only if $\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{MT}} (\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\alpha}, \mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\beta}) = 1.$
\vspace{0.3cm}
<!-- end head-3 -->
<!-- head-4: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal M$ be a finite von Neumann algebra, and let $\mathcal N,\mathcal P,\mathcal Q$ be $\mathrm{II}_1$-subfactors of $\mathcal M$ such that
\[
\begin{array}{ccc}
    \mathcal P & \subset & \mathcal M \\
    \cup && \cup \\
    \mathcal N & \subset & \mathcal Q
\end{array}
\]
is a commuting square. Suppose that the index of at least one of the inclusions $\mathcal N\subseteq\mathcal P$ or $\mathcal N\subseteq\mathcal Q$ belongs to $\{2,3\}\cup[4,\infty]$. Then $\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{KK}}(\mathcal P,\mathcal Q)=1=\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{MT}}(\mathcal P,\mathcal Q)$.
\vspace{0.2cm}
<!-- end head-4 -->
<!-- head-5: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal N \subseteq \mathcal M$ be $\mathrm{II}_1$ subfactors with $[\mathcal{M}:\mathcal{N}]\ge 4$, and let $\mathcal P,\mathcal Q$ be intermediate $\mathrm{II}_1$ subfactors.
    Suppose that
    \[\begin{array}{ccc}
            \mathcal P & \subset & \mathcal M \\
            \cup & & \cup \\
            \mathcal N & \subset & \mathcal Q
        \end{array}
    \]
    is a commuting square. Then
    \[
        \mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{MT}}(\mathcal P,\mathcal Q)=1=\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{KK}}(\mathcal P,\mathcal Q).
    \]
<!-- end head-5 -->
<!-- head-6: body_md -->
Let $u,v\in
  \mathbb{H}^u_{n}\IfValueT{$}{($)}
 with $u\not\sim v$ such that $\mathscr{R}_u\cap\mathscr{R}_v$ is a finite-index subfactor of $\mathscr{R}$.
    If
    \[
        \begin{array}{ccc}
            \mathscr{R}_u & \subset & \mathscr{R} \\
            \cup && \cup \\
            \mathscr{R}_u\cap\mathscr{R}_v & \subset & \mathscr{R}_v
        \end{array}
    \]
    is a commuting square, then
    \[
        \mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{KK}}(\mathscr{R}_u,\mathscr{R}_v)=1=\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{MT}}(\mathscr{R}_u, \mathscr{R}_v).
    \]
<!-- end head-6 -->
<!-- head-7: body_md -->
Let $(\mathcal M, \tau)$ be a finite von Neumann algebra, and let $\mathcal P,\mathcal Q\subseteq \mathcal M$ be diffuse orthogonal subalgebras. Then
\[
\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{KK}}(\mathcal P,\mathcal Q)=1=\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{MT}}(\mathcal P,\mathcal Q).
\]
<!-- end head-7 -->
<!-- head-8: body_md -->
Let $\mathbb{F}_{2}= \langle a, b \rangle$ and consider a unitary $u \in L(\langle b \rangle)$. Then 
    \[
    \mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{MT}} (L(\langle a \rangle), u L(\langle a \rangle)u^*) = \sqrt{1- |\tau(u)|^4}.
    \]
<!-- end head-8 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:comm-sq}
    Let $\mathcal B \subseteq \mathcal C, \mathcal D \subseteq \mathcal A$ be $C^*$-algebras, and let
    \[
        E_{\mathcal B}:\mathcal A\to\mathcal B,\qquad
        E_{\mathcal C}:\mathcal A\to\mathcal C,\qquad
        E_{\mathcal D}:\mathcal A\to\mathcal D
    \]
    be conditional expectations. We say that the quadruple
    $(\mathcal A,\mathcal C,\mathcal D,\mathcal B)$ forms a \emph{commuting square with respect to
    $E_{\mathcal B}$, $E_{\mathcal C}$, and $E_{\mathcal D}$} if
    \[
        E_{\mathcal C}\circ E_{\mathcal D}
        = E_{\mathcal B}
        = E_{\mathcal D}\circ E_{\mathcal C}.
    \]
    We often represent this commuting square by the diagram
    \[
        \begin{array}{ccc}
            \mathcal D & \subset & \mathcal A \\
            \cup & & \cup \\
            \mathcal B & \subset & \mathcal C.
        \end{array}
    \]
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
{\cite[Definition 2.2]{bakshi-etal-2019}}
  Let $(\mathcal N \subseteq \mathcal P, \mathcal Q \subseteq \mathcal M)$ be a quadruple of $\mathrm{II}_1$-factors. The interior angle between $\mathcal P$ and $\mathcal Q$ is defined by
\[
\operatorname{cos}(\alpha_{\mathcal N}^{\mathcal M})(\mathcal P,\mathcal Q)= \frac{\langle e_{\mathcal P}- e_{\mathcal N}, e_{\mathcal Q}-e_{\mathcal N}\rangle_{\tau}}{\|e_{\mathcal P}- e_{\mathcal N}\|_{\tau}\|e_{\mathcal Q}- e_{\mathcal N}\|_{\tau}},
\]
where $e_{\mathcal P}$, $e_{\mathcal Q}$, and $e_{\mathcal N}$ denote the corresponding Jones projections, and $\tau$ denotes the unique faithful normal trace on $\mathcal M$.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\[
    \mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{KK}}(\mathcal Y,\mathcal Z)
    :=\max\left\{
    \sup_{y\in\left( \mathcal Y\right)_1}d(y,\left( \mathcal Z\right)_1),
    \sup_{z\in\left( \mathcal Z\right)_1}d(z,\left( \mathcal Y\right)_1)
    \right\}.
    \]
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{KK-facts}
  Let $\mathcal X$ be a normed space. The following facts about the Kadison--Kastler distance are well known:
  \begin{enumerate}
    \item[(i)] $0\le\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{KK}}(\mathcal Y,\mathcal Z)\le1$ for all subspaces $\mathcal Y,\mathcal Z$ of $\mathcal X$.
    \item[(ii)] $\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{KK}}$ is a metric on the collection of all subspaces of $\mathcal X$ (see \cite[\S~I.4]{viro-topo}).
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\label{def:concrete_definiton}
    For any pair $\mathcal P, \mathcal Q $ of subalgebras of $(\mathcal M, \tau)$, the Mashood-Taylor distance between
$\mathcal P$ and $\mathcal Q$ is defined as
\begin{equation}\label{dMT-expresssion}
\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{MT}}(\mathcal P, \mathcal Q) = d_{H, \|\cdot\|_\tau } \Big(\eta(\left( \mathcal P\right)_1), \eta(\left( \mathcal Q\right)_1)\Big)
= \max \left \{\sup_{\xi\in \eta(\left( P\right)_1)} \operatorname{dist}(\xi, \eta(\left( Q\right)_1)), \sup_{\zeta\in \eta(\left( Q\right)_1)}\operatorname{dist}(\zeta, \eta(\left( P\right)_1))\right\}
\end{equation}
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
Let $(\mathcal M, \tau)$ be a finite von Neumann algebra. The following elementary facts are well-known; for a proof, see, for instance, \cite[Lemma 5.6]{Gupta_kumar_2024}:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item[(i)] $\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{MT}}$ is a semi-metric on the collection of subalgebras of $\mathcal M$.
    \item[(ii)] $\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{MT}}$ is a metric on the collection of von Neumann subalgebras of $\mathcal M$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- prop-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:best_approximation}
 Let $(\mathcal M, \tau)$ be a finite von Neumann algebra and $\mathcal N$ be a von Neumann subalgebra with common unit. Then,
 \[
 \operatorname{dist} \Big(\eta(x), \eta(\left( \mathcal N\right)_1)\Big)= \|\eta(x)- \eta(E_{\mathcal N}(x))\|_{\tau} =  \operatorname{dist} \Big(\eta(x), L^{2}(\mathcal N)\Big)
\]
for all $x  \in \left( \mathcal M\right)_1$, where $\operatorname{dist} \Big(\eta(x), \eta(\left( \mathcal N\right)_1)\Big)= \inf_{z\in \left( \mathcal N\right)_1}\|\eta(x)-\eta(z)\|_{\tau}$.
<!-- end prop-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Let $x \in \left( \mathcal M\right)_1$. Since $\eta(\left( \mathcal N\right)_1)$ is complete (see \cite[Proposition 2.6.4]{Anantharaman_Popa_1986}) and convex in $L^{2}(\mathcal M, \tau)$, there exists
a unique $y_0 \in \left( \mathcal N\right)_1$ such that
\(
\|\eta(x)- \eta(y_0)\|_{\tau}= \operatorname{dist} (\eta(x), \eta(\left( \mathcal N\right)_1)).
\)  We assert that   $y_0= E_{\mathcal N}(x).$

Let $e_{\mathcal N}: L^{2}(\mathcal M) \rightarrow L^{2}(\mathcal N):=
\overline{\eta(\mathcal N})^{\|.\|_{\tau}}$ be the Jones projection. Then,
it is known that
\(
\|e_{\mathcal N}(\eta(w))- \eta(w)\|_{\tau}= \operatorname{dist} (\eta(w), L^2(\mathcal N))
\)
for all $w \in \mathcal M$. In particular, for above $x \in \left( \mathcal M\right)_1$,
\[
\|\eta(E_{\mathcal N}(x))- \eta(x)\|_{\tau}= \|e_{\mathcal N}(\eta(x))-
\eta(x)\|_{\tau}= \operatorname{dist} (\eta(x), L^2(\mathcal N)).
\]
Moreover,   $E_{\mathcal N}(x)\in \left( \mathcal N\right)_1$ because   $x \in \left( \mathcal M\right)_1$. So, 
\[
\operatorname{dist} (\eta(x), \eta(\left( \mathcal N\right)_1))= \|\eta(x)- \eta(y_0)\|_{\tau} \leq \|\eta(x)- \eta(E_{\mathcal N}(x))\|_{\tau}= \operatorname{dist} (\eta(x), L^2(\mathcal N))\leq \operatorname{dist} (\eta(x), \eta(\left( \mathcal N\right)_1)).
\]
Thus, by the uniqueness of the best approximation element $\eta(y_0)$ of
$\eta(x)$ in $\eta(\left( \mathcal N\right)_1)$, we get \( y_0= E_{\mathcal N}(x)\). This proves
our assertion. In particular, we also observe that 
\[
\operatorname{dist} (\eta(x),
\eta(\left( \mathcal N\right)_1))= \|\eta(x)- \eta(E_{\mathcal N}(x))\|_{\tau}=  \operatorname{dist} (\eta(x), L^{2}(\mathcal N)),
\]
as was desired.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:mashood_taylor}
Let $(\mathcal M, \tau)$ be a finite von Neumann algebra. Then for any von Neumann subalgebras $\mathcal P$ and $\mathcal Q$, we have 
\[
\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{MT}}(\mathcal P, \mathcal Q)= \max \left \{\sup_{x\in \left( \mathcal P\right)_1}\|\eta (x)-\eta(E_{\mathcal Q}(x))\|_{\tau}, \sup_{z\in \left( \mathcal Q\right)_1}\|\eta(z)-\eta(E_{\mathcal P}(z))\|_{\tau}\right\}
\]
where $E_{\mathcal P}$ and $E_{\mathcal Q}$ are the unique trace preserving conditional expectation from $\mathcal M $ onto $\mathcal P$ and $\mathcal Q$ respectively.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- prop-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:mt_and_kk} 
Let $(\mathcal M, \tau)$ be a finite von Neumann algebra. Then for any two subalgebras  $\mathcal P$ and $\mathcal Q$ of $\mathcal M$,
 \[
 \mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{MT}} (\mathcal P, \mathcal Q) \leq \mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{KK}}(\mathcal P, \mathcal Q).
 \]
<!-- end prop-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
The proof follows from the following well-known fact that for any $x\in \mathcal M$,
    \[
    \|\eta(x)\|_{\tau}\leq \|x\|_{op}.
    \]
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lem-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:jones-proj-mn-gen}
    Let $\eta_k : 
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{^}{(^)}
{\otimes k} \to L^2(
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{^}{(^)}
{\otimes k}, \tau_k)$ be the canonical inclusion mapping the algebra into its GNS Hilbert space. The Jones projection $e_k$ decomposes as $\operatorname{id}_{L^2(
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{^}{(^)}
{\otimes (k-1)})} \otimes e_1$, where $e_1$ is the Jones projection for the base case $\mathbb{C}\cong \mathbb{C} \mathbb{I}_n \subseteq 
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{$}{($)}
.
<!-- end lem-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
By the standard properties of the GNS construction for tensor products of matrix algebras, the Hilbert space factorizes up to unitary equivalence
    $$L^2\left(
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{^}{(^)}
{\otimes k}, \tau_k\right) \cong L^2\left(
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{^}{(^)}
{\otimes (k-1)}, \tau_{k-1}\right) \otimes L^2(
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{,}{(,)}
 \tau_1).$$
    
    Under this identification, for any elementary tensor $x \otimes y \in 
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{^}{(^)}
{\otimes (k-1)} \otimes 
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{$}{($)}
, the canonical inclusion factors as
    $$\eta_k(x \otimes y) = \eta_{k-1}(x) \otimes \eta_1(y).$$
    
    The trace-preserving conditional expectation $E_k : 
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{^}{(^)}
{\otimes (k-1)} \otimes 
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{\to}{(\to)}
 
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{^}{(^)}
{\otimes (k-1)} \otimes \mathbb{C}$ operates by taking the trace of the second tensor factor, i.e.
    $$E_k(x \otimes y) = x \otimes \tau_1(y)\mathbb{I}_n.$$
    
    where $\mathbb{I}_n$ is the identity matrix in $
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{$}{($)}
.
    
    By definition, the Jones projection $e_k$ is the orthogonal projection onto the closed subspace generated by $\eta_k\left(
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{^}{(^)}
{\otimes (k-1)}\right)$. Its action on the dense subspace $\eta_k\left(
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{^}{(^)}
{\otimes k}\right)$ is characterized by $e_k \eta_k(m) = \eta_k(E_k(m))$ for all $m \in 
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{^}{(^)}
{\otimes k}$. Applying this to elementary tensors yields
    $$e_k(\eta_{k-1}(x) \otimes \eta_1(y)) = \eta_k(E_k(x \otimes y)) = \eta_k(x \otimes \tau_1(y)\mathbb{I}_n) = \eta_{k-1}(x) \otimes \eta_1(\tau_1(y)\mathbb{I}_n).$$
    
    Observe that the action leaves the first tensor factor $\eta_{k-1}(x)$ completely invariant. On the second factor, the map $\eta_1(y) \mapsto \eta_1(\tau_1(y)\mathbb{I}_n)$ is precisely the action of the Jones projection $e_1$ corresponding to the conditional expectation $E_1 : 
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{\to}{(\to)}
 \mathbb{C}$ from the base case. Therefore, as an operator on $L^2\left(
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{^}{(^)}
{\otimes (k-1)}, \tau_{k-1}\right) \otimes L^2(
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{,}{(,)}
 \tau_1)$, we have $e_k = \operatorname{id}_{L^2\left(
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{^}{(^)}
{\otimes (k-1)}, \tau_{k-1} \right)} \otimes e_1$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lem-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:hyperfinite-ii-1-basic-cons}
    Let $k \ge 1$ be an integer. Consider the unital inclusion of finite-dimensional von Neumann algebras $
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{^}{(^)}
{\otimes (k-1)}\subseteq 
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{^}{(^)}
{\otimes k}$, formed by the canonical identification $
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{^}{(^)}
{\otimes (k-1)} \cong 
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{^}{(^)}
{\otimes (k-1)} \otimes \mathbb{C} \subseteq 
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{^}{(^)}
{\otimes (k-1)} \otimes 
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{$}{($)}
. Let $\tau_k$ be the canonical normalized trace on $
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{^}{(^)}
{\otimes k}$, and $E_k: 
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{^}{(^)}
{\otimes k} \to 
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{^}{(^)}
{\otimes (k-1)}$ be the unique $\tau_k$-preserving conditional expectation. Then the Jones basic construction $\langle 
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{^}{(^)}
{\otimes k}, e_k \rangle$ is spatially isomorphic to $
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{^}{(^)}
{\otimes (k+1)}$.
<!-- end lem-2 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal M:= 
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{^}{(^)}
{\otimes k}$ and $\mathcal A := 
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{^}{(^)}
{\otimes (k-1)}$
    The Jones basic construction algebra, denoted $\langle \mathcal M, e_k \rangle$, is the von Neumann algebra acting on $L^2\left(\mathcal M, \tau_k\right)$ generated by $\mathcal M$ (acting by left multiplication) and the Jones projection $e_k$.
    
    From the factorization $\mathcal M = \mathcal A \otimes 
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{$}{($)}
 and Lemma \ref{lem:jones-proj-mn-gen}, we can write the generators of the basic construction as
    $$\langle \mathcal M, e_k \rangle = \left( (\mathcal A \otimes 
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{)}{())}
 \cup \{ \operatorname{id}_{L^2(\mathcal A)} \otimes e_1 \} \right)''.$$
    
    Because the operators in $\mathcal A$ act strictly on the first Hilbert space factor $L^2(\mathcal A, \tau_{k-1})$, and the operators in $
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{$}{($)}
 along with the projection $e_1$ act strictly on the second Hilbert space factor $L^2(
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{,}{(,)}
 \tau_1)$. Thus, we have
    $$\langle \mathcal M, e_k \rangle \cong \mathcal A \otimes \langle 
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{,}{(,)}
 e_1 \rangle.$$
   
    Now the basic construction for the inclusion $\mathbb{C} \subseteq 
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{$}{($)}
 (see \cite[Theorem 5.1]{ghoshkumar-kk2026}) yields:
    $$\langle 
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{,}{(,)}
 e_1 \rangle \cong 
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{\otimes}{(\otimes)}
 
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{.}{(.)}
$$
    
    Hence, we get
    $$\langle \mathcal M, e_k \rangle \cong 
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{^}{(^)}
{\otimes (k-1)} \otimes (
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{\otimes}{(\otimes)}
 
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{)}{())}
\cong 
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{^}{(^)}
{\otimes (k+1)}.$$
    
    This completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- lem-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:index-invariance}
 For each $k \ge 0$, consider the inclusion
$
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{^}{(^)}
{\otimes k} \subseteq^{E_k} 
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{^}{(^)}
{\otimes (k+1)}$,
where $E_k$ denotes the canonical trace-preserving conditional expectation, characterized by
\(    \tau_k \circ E_k = \tau_{k+1}. 
   \)   
   Then $\operatorname{Ind}(\widetilde{E_k})= \operatorname{Ind}(E_0)$ for each $k$, where $\widetilde{E_k}$ is the Watatani dual coditional expectation corresponding to $E_k$.
<!-- end lem-3 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
It follows from \cite[Proposition 2.3.4]{watatani1990}.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lem-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:dual-exp-mn}
For each $k \ge 1$, consider the inclusion
$
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{^}{(^)}
{\otimes k} \subseteq^{E_k} 
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{^}{(^)}
{\otimes (k+1)}$,
where $E_k$ denotes the canonical trace-preserving conditional expectation, characterized by
\(    \tau_{k+1} \circ E_k = \tau_{k+1}.
   \)
Then the Watatani dual conditional expectation $\widetilde{E_k}$ preserves the canonical normalized trace $\tau_{k+2}$. That is, $\tau_{k+1} \circ \tilde{E}_k = \tau_{k+2}$.
<!-- end lem-4 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Let $M_k = \mathbb{M}_n^{\otimes k}$. The inclusion $M_k \subseteq M_{k+1}$ is canonically identified as $x \mapsto x \otimes \mathbb{I}_n$.

    The canonical trace-preserving conditional expectation $E_k: \mathbb{M}_n^{\otimes (k+1)} \to \mathbb{M}_n^{\otimes k}$ is given by 
    $$E_k(x \otimes y) = x \otimes \tau_1(y)\mathbb{I}_n$$
   for $x \in \mathbb{M}_n^{\otimes k}$, $y \in \mathbb{M}_n$ and $M_k$ is identified with $M_k \otimes \mathbb{C}\mathbb{I}_n$. 
    
Since elements of the form $x e_{k+1} y$ span $M_{k+2}$ for all $x,y \in M_{k+1}$, it suffices to verify the trace-preserving property on these elements. First, let us evaluate the left-hand side. Applying $\tau_{k+1}$ to the definition of $\tilde{E}_k$ and using Lemma \ref{lem:index-invariance} and trace preserving property of $E_k$, we get
    $$\tau_{k+1}(\tilde{E}_k(x e_{k+1} y)) =  \tau_{k+1}\left((\operatorname{Ind}(E_0))^{-1}E_{k}(xy)\right)=\tau_{k+1}\left(\frac{1}{n^2} x y\right) = \frac{1}{n^2} \tau_{k+1}(xy).$$

    Now, let us evaluate the right-hand side, $\tau_{k+2}(x e_{k+1} y)$. Using the trace property of $\tau_{k+2}$, we get $$\tau_{k+2}(x e_{k+1} y) = \tau_{k+2}(yx e_{k+1}).$$

    We now evaluate the trace of $w e_{k+1}$ for any $w \in M_{k+1}$. The $M_{k+2}$ can be decomposes as $\mathbb{M}_n^{\otimes k} \otimes (\mathbb{M}_n \otimes \mathbb{M}_n)$, and by the Lemma \ref{lem:jones-proj-mn-gen} the projection is $e_{k+1} = \mathbb{I}_{n^k} \otimes e_1$. A general element $w \in M_{k+1}$ takes the form $a \otimes (b \otimes \mathbb{I}_n)$.

    Thus, $w e_{k+1}$ decomposes over the tensor product as $a \otimes ((b \otimes \mathbb{I}_n)e_1)$. Evaluating the trace yields:
    $$\tau_{k+2}(w e_{k+1}) = \tau_k(a) \cdot \tau_2((b \otimes \mathbb{I}_n)e_1).$$

    Using the trace property in $M_2$ and the fact that $e_1$ is a projection ($e_1^2 = e_1$), we get
    $$\tau_2((b \otimes \mathbb{I}_n)e_1) = \tau_2(e_1 (b \otimes \mathbb{I}_n) e_1).$$
    
    By the defining property of the Jones projection, $e_1 (b \otimes \mathbb{I}_n) e_1 = E_1(b) e_1 = \tau_1(b)e_1$. Therefore
    $$\tau_2(e_1 (b \otimes \mathbb{I}_n) e_1) = \tau_2(\tau_1(b)e_1) = \tau_1(b)\tau_2(e_1).$$

    Because $e_1$ is a rank-1 projection in $\mathbb{M}_n \otimes \mathbb{M}_n \cong \mathbb{M}_{n^2}$, its normalized trace is $\frac{1}{n^2}$. Substituting this back gives:
    $$\tau_{k+2}(w e_{k+1}) = \tau_k(a) \tau_1(b) \frac{1}{n^2} = \tau_{k+1}(w) \frac{1}{n^2}.$$

    Letting $w = yx$, we obtain,
    $$\tau_{k+2}(x e_{k+1} y) = \frac{1}{n^2} \tau_{k+1}(yx)= \tau_{k+1}(xy).$$
    Thus, we get
    $$\tau_{k+1}(\tilde{E}_k(x e_{k+1} y)) = \tau_{k+2}(x e_{k+1} y).$$
    This completes the proof!
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- prop-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:jones-tower-for-hyperfin-ii-1}
Consider the unital inclusion $\mathbb{C}\mathbb{I}_n \subseteq^{E_0} 
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{$}{($)}
, where $E_0 = \frac{1}{n}\operatorname{Tr} \otimes \mathbb{I}_n.$ The infinite Jones tower obtained by iteratively applying the Jones basic construction is given by the sequence
\[
\mathbb{C} \subseteq^{E_0}_{e_1} 
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{\subseteq}{(\subseteq)}
^{E_1}_{e_2} 
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{^}{(^)}
{\otimes 2}
\subseteq \cdots
\subseteq 
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{^}{(^)}
{\otimes k}
\subseteq^{E_k}_{e_{k+1}} 
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{^}{(^)}
{\otimes (k+1)}
\subseteq \cdots,
\]
where, for each $k \geq 0$, $E_k$ denotes the canonical trace-preserving conditional expectation and the corresponding Jones projection is given by $e_{k+1}
=
\operatorname{id}_{L^2(
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{^}{(^)}
{\otimes k})} \otimes e_1.$ Moreover the Watatani's dual conditional expectation, $\widetilde{E_k}= E_{k+1}$.
<!-- end prop-3 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Follows from Lemma \ref{lem:jones-proj-mn-gen}, Lemma \ref{lem:hyperfinite-ii-1-basic-cons} and Lemma \ref{lem:dual-exp-mn}.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- prop-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:nic-tower}
Consider the unital inclusion $\Delta^{(n)}\subseteq^{E_{\Delta^{(n)}}} 
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{$}{($)}
, where $E_{\Delta^{(n)}}$ is the canonical $\operatorname{Tr}$ preserving conditional expectation. The infinite Jones tower obtained by iteratively applying the Jones basic construction is given by the sequence
    \[
    \Delta^{(n)}\subseteq_{e_2} 
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{\subseteq}{(\subseteq)}
_{e_3}
    \cdots
    \subseteq
    
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{^}{(^)}
{\otimes (k-1)} \otimes \Delta^{(n)}
    \subseteq_{e_{2k}}
    
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{^}{(^)}
{\otimes k}
    \subseteq_{e_{2k+1}}
    
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{^}{(^)}
{\otimes k} \otimes \Delta^{(n)}
    \subseteq \cdots
    \]
    Where the corresponding Jones projection $e_j$ is given recursively by
    \begin{align*}
        e_2 &:= \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i,j=1}^n E_{ij}, \quad
        e_3 := \sum_{i=1}^n (E_{ii} \otimes E_{ii}), \\
        e_{2k} &:= \bigotimes_{1}^{k-1} (\mathbb{I}_n \otimes e_2), \quad
        e_{2k+1} := \bigotimes_{1}^{k-1} (\mathbb{I}_n \otimes e_3),
        \qquad k=2,3,\dots.
    \end{align*}
<!-- end prop-4 -->
<!-- prop-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:nic-unitary-tower}
    Let $u$ be an $n\times n$ Hadamard unitary in $
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{$}{($)}
. Consider the unital inclusion $u\Delta^{(n)} u^* \subseteq^{E_u} 
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{$}{($)}
, where $E_u:= \operatorname{Ad}_u \circ E_{\Delta^{(n)}} \circ \operatorname{Ad}_{u^*}$. The infinite Jones tower obtained by iteratively applying the Jones basic construction is given by the sequence
    \[
    u\Delta^{(n)} u^*
    \subseteq_{e_2}u_1 
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{u}{(u)}
_1^*\subseteq \cdots
    \subseteq
    u_{2k-1}
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{^}{(^)}
{\otimes k}(u_{2k-1})^*
    \subseteq_{e_{2k+1}}
    u_{2k}(
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{^}{(^)}
{\otimes k}\otimes\Delta^{(n)})(u_{2k})^*
    \subseteq_{e_{2k+2}} \cdots.
    \]
    Here, $u_{2k-1}\in 
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{^}{(^)}
{\otimes k}\otimes\Delta^{(n)}$ and
    $u_{2k}\in
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{^}{(^)}
{\otimes(k+1)}$ are unitaries defined recursively by
    \begin{align*}
        D_u := \sqrt{n}\sum_{i,j=1}^n
        \overline{u_{ij}}(E_{jj}\otimes E_{ii}), &\quad
        u_1 := (u\otimes\mathbb{I}_n)D_u,\\
        u_{2k} := u_{2k-1}
        \left(\otimes^k\mathbb{I}_n\otimes u\right),
        &\quad
        u_{2k+1} := \prod_{i=0}^k
        \left(\otimes^i\mathbb{I}_n\otimes u_1\otimes^{k-i}\mathbb{I}_n\right),
        \quad k=1,2,\dots.
    \end{align*}
    The Jones projections $e_k$ are the same as those defined in the preceding proposition.
<!-- end prop-5 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
\label{def:spin-model-subfactor}
    Let $u \in 
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{$}{($)}
 be a Hadamard unitary. The \emph{spin model subfactor}, denoted by $\mathscr{R}_u$, is defined as the hyperfinite $\mathrm{II}_1$ factor obtained by taking the weak closure of the inductive limit of the unitarily twisted Jones tower constructed in Proposition \ref{prop:nic-unitary-tower} with respect to the unique canonical normalized trace. 
    
    Similarly, the ambient hyperfinite $\mathrm{II}_1$ factor, denoted by $\mathscr{R}$, is defined as the weak closure of the inductive limit of the standard, untwisted Jones tower for the inclusion $\Delta^{(n)} \subseteq 
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{$}{($)}
 given in Proposition \ref{prop:nic-tower}. By construction, $\mathscr{R}_u \subseteq \mathscr{R}$.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- prop-6: body_md -->
Let $M_{k-1} \subseteq M_k \subseteq M_{k+1} = \langle M_k, e_{k+1} \rangle$ be any two consecutive inclusions in the unitarily twisted Jones tower defined in Proposition \ref{prop:nic-unitary-tower}, where $[M_k : M_{k-1}] = n$. Let $\tau$ denote the canonical faithful normalized trace on the ambient matrix algebras. Then Watatani's dual conditional expectation $\tilde{E}_k : M_{k+1} \to M_k$ preserves the trace $\tau$, and consequently, $\tilde{E}_k$ coincides exactly with the unique canonical $\tau$-preserving conditional expectation $E_k : M_{k+1} \to M_k$.
<!-- end prop-6 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
By the definition of the Jones basic construction, the algebra $M_{k+1}$ is linearly spanned by elements of the form $x e_{k+1} y$, where $x, y \in M_k$.

    Watatani's dual conditional expectation $\tilde{E}_k : M_{k+1} \to M_k$ is uniquely defined on these spanning elements by
    $$\tilde{E}_k(x e_{k+1} y) = \frac{1}{[M_k : M_{k-1}]} x y = \frac{1}{n} x y$$

    According to Proposition \ref{prop:nic-unitary-tower}, the Jones projections $e_{k+1}$ in this unitarily twisted tower are identically equal to the Jones projections in the standard tower (Proposition \ref{prop:nic-tower}).

    Because the canonical normalized trace $\tau$ on the ambient matrix algebra is unitarily invariant (i.e., $\tau(u X u^*) = \tau(X)$), the spatial rotations defining $M_k$ do not alter the trace values. Furthermore, since the projections $e_{k+1}$ are exactly the standard ones, they maintain the standard Markov property with respect to $\tau$ and the algebra $M_k$.

    Specifically, for any $x, y \in M_k$, the trace satisfies the Markov relation with parameter $\frac{1}{n}$:$$\tau(x e_{k+1} y) = \frac{1}{n} \tau(xy)$$

    We now verify that Watatani's dual expectation $\tilde{E}_k$ preserves $\tau$. Applying the trace to the output of $\tilde{E}_k$ for a generic spanning element and using Lemma \ref{lem:index-invariance}, we get
    $$\tau(\tilde{E}_k(x e_{k+1} y)) = \tau\left( \frac{1}{n} x y \right) = \frac{1}{n} \tau(xy).$$
    Comparing this with the Markov property established above, we get
    $$\tau(\tilde{E}_k(x e_{k+1} y)) = \tau(x e_{k+1} y)$$By linearity, this equality extends to finite sums of such elements. Since these elements span $M_{k+1}$, we conclude that for all $z \in M_{k+1}$:$$\tau(\tilde{E}_k(z)) = \tau(z)$$Thus, Watatani's dual conditional expectation is trace-preserving.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
Two Hadamard unitaries $u,v\in
  \mathbb{H}^u_{n}\IfValueT{$}{($)}
 are said to be \emph{Hadamard equivalent}, denoted by $u\sim_{\mathrm{h}} v$, if there exist diagonal unitaries $D_1,D_2\in
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{$}{($)}
 and permutation matrices $P_1,P_2\in
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{$}{($)}
 such that
    \[
        v=D_1P_1uP_2D_2.
    \]
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
\label{def:bakshi-guin-eq-relation}
    Two Hadamard unitaries $u,v\in
  \mathbb{H}^u_{n}\IfValueT{$}{($)}
 are said to be \emph{equivalent in the sense of Bakshi and Guin}, denoted by $u\sim v$, if there exist a permutation matrix $P$ and a diagonal unitary matrix $D$ such that
    \[
        v=uPD.
    \]
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:bakshi-guin}
Let $\alpha,\beta\in[0,\pi)$ be distinct. Then there exists an involutive
outer automorphism $\Theta_{\alpha,\beta}\in\operatorname{Out}(\mathscr{R})$, that is,
\[
(\Theta_{\alpha,\beta})^2=\operatorname{id}_{\mathscr{R}},
\]
such that,
\begin{align*}
\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\alpha}\cap\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\beta}
&\cong
\left\{
\begin{pmatrix}
x & 0\\
0 & \Theta_{\alpha,\beta}(x)
\end{pmatrix}
:x\in\mathscr{R}
\right\},\\[1ex]
\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\beta}
&\cong
\left\{
\begin{pmatrix}
x & y\\
\Theta_{\alpha,\beta}(y) & \Theta_{\alpha,\beta}(x)
\end{pmatrix}
:x,y\in\mathscr{R}
\right\},\\[1ex]
\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\alpha}
&\cong
\begin{pmatrix}
1&0\\
0&e^{i(\alpha-\beta)}
\end{pmatrix}
\left\{
\begin{pmatrix}
x & y\\
\Theta_{\alpha,\beta}(y) & \Theta_{\alpha,\beta}(x)
\end{pmatrix}
:x,y\in\mathscr{R}
\right\}
\begin{pmatrix}
1&0\\
0&e^{-i(\alpha-\beta)}
\end{pmatrix}.
\end{align*}
Here, all the algebras on the right-hand side are regarded as subalgebras
of $\mn{2}[\mathscr{R}]$.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- lem-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:trace-preserving}
  Let  $\mathcal M$ be a $\mathrm{II}_1$-factor with the  unique faithful normal trace $\tau_{\mathcal M}$ and let  $\Theta\in \operatorname{Aut}(\mathcal M)$ such that $\Theta^2= \operatorname{id}$. Then, $\Theta$ is trace preserving and for any $x,y \in \mathcal M$ 
  $$\tau_{\mathcal M}(\Theta(x)y) = \tau_{\mathcal M}(x\Theta(y)).$$
<!-- end lem-5 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Let $\Theta \in \operatorname{Aut}(\mathcal M)$. We can define a new functional on $\mathcal M$ by composing the trace with this automorphism
    $$\tau'(x) := \tau_{\mathcal M}(\Theta(x)).$$
    Clearly this is faithful, normal  functional. It is a normalized trace because $$\tau'(1) = \tau_{\mathcal M}(\Theta(1)) = \tau_{\mathcal M}(1) = 1.$$
    Also it satisfies the trace property: $\tau'(xy) = \tau_{\mathcal M}(\Theta(xy)) = \tau_{\mathcal M}(\Theta(x)\Theta(y)) = \tau_{\mathcal M}(\Theta(y)\Theta(x)) = \tau_{\mathcal M}(\Theta(yx)) = \tau'(yx)$. Because the normalized trace on a II$_1$ factor is unique, it implies that $\tau' = \tau_{\mathcal M}$. Therefore, $\tau_{\mathcal M}(\Theta(x)) =\tau'(x)= \tau_{\mathcal M}(x)$ for all $x \in \mathcal M$. This implies that $\Theta$ is trace preserving. Let $x,y \in \mathcal M$. Then, we get
  \[
  \tau_{\mathcal M}(\Theta(x)y) = \tau_{\mathcal M}(\Theta(\Theta(x)y))= \tau_{\mathcal M}(\Theta(\Theta(x))\Theta(y))= \tau_{\mathcal M}(x\Theta(y)).
  \]
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- lem-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:condit-exp}
Let $\alpha,\beta\in[0,\pi)$ be distinct and $\Theta_{\alpha, \beta}\in \operatorname{Out}(\mathscr{R})$ as given by Theroem \ref{thm:bakshi-guin}. Then the unique trace-preserving conditional expectations $E_{\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\alpha}}: \mathbb{M}_2(\mathscr{R}) \to \mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_{\alpha}}$ and $E_{\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\beta}}: \mathbb{M}_2(\mathscr{R}) \to \mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\beta}$ are given as follows:

$$E_{\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\alpha}}\left( \begin{bmatrix} m_{11} & m_{12} \\ m_{21} & m_{22} \end{bmatrix} \right) = \begin{bmatrix} x & y e^{i(\beta-\alpha)} \\ \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (y) e^{i(\alpha-\beta)} & \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (x) \end{bmatrix}$$
where $x = \frac{1}{2}(m_{11} + \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (m_{22}))$ and $y = \frac{1}{2}(e^{i(\alpha-\beta)}m_{12} + e^{i(\beta-\alpha)}\Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (m_{21}))$, and
$$E_{\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\beta}}\left( \begin{bmatrix} m_{11} & m_{12} \\ m_{21} & m_{22} \end{bmatrix} \right) = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{m_{11} + \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (m_{22})}{2} & \frac{m_{12} + \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (m_{21})}{2} \\ \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} \left(\frac{m_{12} + \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (m_{21})}{2}\right) & \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} \left(\frac{m_{11} + \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (m_{22})}{2}\right) \end{bmatrix}$$
where $m=\begin{bmatrix} m_{11} & m_{12} \\ m_{21} & m_{22} \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{M}_2(\mathscr{R})$.
<!-- end lem-6 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Let 
 $m=\begin{bmatrix} m_{11} & m_{12} \\ m_{21} & m_{22} \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{M}_2(\mathscr{R})$ be given. The unique normalized trace on $\mathbb{M}_2(\mathscr{R})$ is given by $\tau_{\mathbb{M}_2(\mathscr{R})}(m) = \frac{1}{2}(\tau_{\mathscr{R}}(m_{11}) + \tau_{\mathscr{R}}(m_{22}))$ where $\tau_{\mathscr{R}}$ is the unique trace on $\mathscr{R}$. Since $\mathscr{R}$ is a $\mathrm{II}_1$-factor and $\Theta_{\alpha, \beta}  \in \operatorname{Aut}(\mathscr{R})$ is an automorphism such that $\Theta_{\alpha, \beta} ^2= \operatorname{id}$, then by Lemma \ref{lem:trace-preserving}, $\Theta_{\alpha, \beta} $ is trace-preserving and satisfies $\tau_{\mathscr{R}}(\Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (a)b) = \tau_{\mathscr{R}}(a\Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (b))$ for all $a, b \in \mathscr{R}$. 
 
 
 Let $r= \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (b) & \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (a) \end{bmatrix} \in \mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\beta}$ be an arbitrary element. Then we get 
 $$\tau_{\mathbb{M}_2(\mathscr{R})}((m - E_{\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\beta}}(m))r) = 0.$$ 
 Equating $\tau_{\mathbb{M}_2(\mathscr{R})}(mr) = \tau_{\mathbb{M}_2(\mathscr{R})}(E_{\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\beta}}(m)r)$ gives
 $$\frac{1}{2}\tau_{\mathscr{R}}(m_{11}a + m_{12}\Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (b) + m_{21}b + m_{22}\Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (a)) = \frac{1}{2}\tau_{\mathscr{R}}(xa + y\Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (b) + \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (y)b + \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (x)\Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (a)).$$
 Using the property $\tau_{\mathscr{R}}(\Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (u)v) = \tau_\mathscr{R}(u\Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (v))$ and $\Theta_{\alpha, \beta} ^2 = \operatorname{id}$, the right side simplifies to $\tau_\mathscr{R}(xa + y\Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (b))$. The left side rearranges to $\frac{1}{2}\tau_\mathscr{R}((m_{11} + \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (m_{22}))a + (m_{12} + \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (m_{21}))\Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (b))$.
 Since this must hold for all $a, b \in \mathscr{R}$, we can equate the terms: $x = \frac{1}{2}(m_{11} + \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (m_{22}))$, $y = \frac{1}{2}(m_{12} + \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (m_{21}))$. Therefore, the expectation is 
 $$E_{\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\beta}}\left( \begin{bmatrix} m_{11} & m_{12} \\ m_{21} & m_{22} \end{bmatrix} \right) = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{m_{11} + \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (m_{22})}{2} & \frac{m_{12} + \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (m_{21})}{2} \\ \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} \left(\frac{m_{12} + \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (m_{21})}{2}\right) & \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} \left(\frac{m_{11} + \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (m_{22})}{2}\right) \end{bmatrix}.$$ 
 Similarly, take an arbitrary element in $\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\alpha}$ and apply the exact same trace-orthogonality procedure. The diagonal terms behave identically to $\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\beta}$, yielding the exact same expression for $x$. For the off-diagonal terms, factoring in the phase shift $e^{i(\beta-\alpha)}$ and its conjugate $e^{i(\alpha-\beta)}$, the trace equivalence demands that
 $$y = \frac{1}{2} \left( e^{i(\alpha-\beta)}m_{12} + e^{i(\beta-\alpha)}\Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (m_{21}) \right).$$
 Thus, the conditional expectation onto $\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\alpha}$ is
 $$E_{\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\alpha}}\left( \begin{bmatrix} m_{11} & m_{12} \\ m_{21} & m_{22} \end{bmatrix} \right) = \begin{bmatrix} x & y e^{i(\beta-\alpha)} \\ \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (y) e^{i(\alpha-\beta)} & \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (x) \end{bmatrix}$$
 where the parameters are 
 $$x = \frac{1}{2}(m_{11} + \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (m_{22}))$$
 $$y = \frac{1}{2}(e^{i(\alpha-\beta)}m_{12} + e^{i(\beta-\alpha)}\Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (m_{21})).$$
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- lem-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:one-sided-spin}
Let $\alpha,\beta\in[0,\pi)$ be distinct and $\Theta_{\alpha, \beta}\in \operatorname{Out}(\mathscr{R})$ as given by Theorem \ref{thm:bakshi-guin}. Let $\tau$ denote the unique normalized trace on $\mathbb{M}_{2}(\mathscr{R})$. Then
$$\sup_{m\in \left( \mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_{\alpha}}\right)_1} \Vert{}\eta(m) - \eta(E_{\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_{\beta}}}(m))\Vert{}_\tau = \vert{}\sin(\beta-\alpha)\vert{}.$$
<!-- end lem-7 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Let $m$ be an arbitrary element in $\left( \mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\alpha}\right)_1$. From the definition of $\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\alpha}$, it has the form, 
$$m = \begin{bmatrix} x & y e^{i(\beta-\alpha)} \\ \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (y) e^{i(\alpha-\beta)} & \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (x) \end{bmatrix} \quad \text{for } x, y \in \mathscr{R}.$$
Using the conditional expectation formula onto $\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\beta}$ from the Lemma \ref{lem:condit-exp}, we substitute the entries of $m$ : $m_{11} = x$, $m_{12} = y e^{i(\beta-\alpha)}$, $m_{21} = \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (y) e^{i(\alpha-\beta)}$, $m_{22} = \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (x)$. The diagonal entries of $E_{\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\beta}}(m)$ are $\frac{1}{2}(x + \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (\Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (x))) = x$ (since $\Theta_{\alpha, \beta} ^2 = \text{id}$). The $(1,2)$ entry is
$$\frac{1}{2}(m_{12} + \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (m_{21})) = \frac{1}{2}\left(y e^{i(\beta-\alpha)} + y e^{i(\alpha-\beta)}\right) = y \cos(\beta-\alpha).$$
Thus, the projection is
$$E_{\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_{\beta}}}(m) = \begin{bmatrix} x & y \cos(\beta-\alpha) \\ \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (y) \cos(\beta-\alpha) & \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (x) \end{bmatrix}.$$

Subtracting the projection $E_{\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_{\beta}}}(m)$ from $m$, we get

\begin{align*}
    z &= \begin{bmatrix} 0 & y(e^{i(\beta-\alpha)} - \cos(\beta-\alpha)) \\ \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (y)(e^{i(\alpha-\beta)} - \cos(\beta-\alpha)) & 0 \end{bmatrix}\\
&= \begin{bmatrix} 0 & i y \sin(\beta-\alpha) \\ -i \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (y) \sin(\beta-\alpha) & 0 \end{bmatrix}.
\end{align*}


First, note that
$$z^* z = \sin^2(\beta-\alpha) \begin{bmatrix} 0 & i \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (y^*) \\ -i y^* & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 0 & i y \\ -i \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (y) & 0 \end{bmatrix} = \sin^2(\beta-\alpha) \begin{bmatrix} \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (y^* y) & 0 \\ 0 & y^* y \end{bmatrix}.$$
We now apply the trace on $
  \mathbb{M}_{2}\IfValueT{\otimes}{(\otimes)}
 \mathscr{R}$, we get
$$\tau(z^* z) = \frac{1}{2} \left[ \tau_\mathscr{R}(\sin^2(\beta-\alpha) \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (y^* y)) + \tau_\mathscr{R}(\sin^2(\beta-\alpha) y^* y) \right].$$
Because $\Theta_{\alpha, \beta} $ is trace-preserving, $\tau_\mathscr{R}(\Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (y^* y)) = \tau_\mathscr{R}(y^* y) = \Vert{}y\Vert{}_{\tau_\mathscr{R}}^2$. Then, we get 
$$\Vert{}\eta(z)\Vert{}_\tau^2 = \sin^2(\beta-\alpha) \Vert{}y\Vert{}_{\tau_\mathscr{R}}^2.$$
Therefore, the $\tau$-norm distance for a given $m$ is
$$\Vert{}\eta(m) - \eta(E_{\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\beta}}(m))\Vert{}_\tau = \vert{}\sin(\beta-\alpha)\vert{} \Vert{}y\Vert{}_{\tau_\mathscr{R}}$$
Since $m$ is in the closed unit ball with respect to the operator norm, this implies $m^* m \le 1_{
  \mathbb{M}_{2}\IfValueT{\otimes}{(\otimes)}
 \mathscr{R}}$. Computing the $(2,2)$ diagonal entry of $m^* m$
$$(m^* m)_{22} = (y e^{i(\beta-\alpha)})^*(y e^{i(\beta-\alpha)}) + \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (x)^*\Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (x) = y^* y + \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (x^* x) \le 1_\mathscr{R}$$
Applying the trace $\tau_\mathscr{R}$ to this inequality gives 
$$\tau_\mathscr{R}(y^* y) + \tau_\mathscr{R}(\Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (x^* x)) \le 1 \implies \Vert{}y\Vert{}_{\tau_\mathscr{R}}^2 + \Vert{}x\Vert{}_{\tau_\mathscr{R}}^2 \le 1.$$
This forces $\Vert{}y\Vert{}_{\tau_\mathscr{R}} \le \sqrt{1 - \Vert{}x\Vert{}_{\tau_\mathscr{R}}^2} \le 1$. Thus, we get
$$\Vert{}\eta(m) - \eta(E_{\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_{\beta}}}(m))\Vert{}_\tau = \vert{}\sin(\beta-\alpha)\vert{} \Vert{}y\Vert{}_{\tau_\mathscr{R}}\leq \vert{}\sin(\beta-\alpha)\vert{}.$$ 
We can construct a specific element $m_0 \in \left( \mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_{\alpha}}\right)_1$ that attains this bound. Choose $x = 0$ and $y = 1_\mathscr{R}$. This gives the matrix
$$m_0 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & e^{i(\beta-\alpha)} 1_\mathscr{R} \\ e^{i(\alpha-\beta)} 1_\mathscr{R} & 0 \end{bmatrix}.$$
$$m_0^* m_0 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & e^{-i(\alpha-\beta)} 1_\mathscr{R} \\ e^{-i(\beta-\alpha)} 1_\mathscr{R} & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 0 & e^{i(\beta-\alpha)} 1_\mathscr{R} \\ e^{i(\alpha-\beta)} 1_\mathscr{R} & 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1_\mathscr{R} & 0 \\ 0 & 1_\mathscr{R} \end{bmatrix} = 1_{
  \mathbb{M}_{2}\IfValueT{\otimes}{(\otimes)}
 \mathscr{R}}.$$
Since $m_0^* m_0$ is the identity, its operator norm is exactly $\Vert{}m_0\Vert{} = 1$, so $m_0 \in \left( \mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_{\alpha}}\right)_1$. Now, we get
$$\Vert{}\eta(m_0) - \eta(E_{\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\beta}}(m_0))\Vert{}_\tau = \vert{}\sin(\beta-\alpha)\vert{} (1) = \vert{}\sin(\beta-\alpha)\vert{}.$$
Therefore, 
$$\sup_{m\in \left( \mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_{\alpha}}\right)_1} \Vert{}\eta(m) - \eta(E_{\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_{\beta}}}(m))\Vert{}_\tau = \vert{}\sin(\beta-\alpha)\vert{}.$$
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- lem-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:other-sided-spin}
    Let $\alpha,\beta\in[0,\pi)$ be distinct and $\Theta_{\alpha, \beta}\in \operatorname{Out}(\mathscr{R})$ as given by Theorem \ref{thm:bakshi-guin}. Let $\tau$ denote the unique normalized trace on $\mathbb{M}_{2}(\mathscr{R})$. Then
    $$\sup_{n\in \left( \mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_{\beta}}\right)_1}\|\eta(n)- \eta(E_{\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_{\alpha}}}(n))\|_{\tau}= \vert{}\sin(\beta-\alpha)\vert{}.$$
<!-- end lem-8 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Let $n \in \left( \mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_{\beta}}\right)_1$. By definition, $n$ has the form
     $$n = \begin{bmatrix} x & y \\ \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (y) & \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (x) \end{bmatrix} \quad \text{for } x, y \in \mathscr{R}.$$
     
     Using the formula in Lemma \ref{lem:condit-exp} for the conditional expectation onto $\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_{\alpha}}$, we substitute the entries of $n$: $n_{11} = x$, $n_{12} = y$, $n_{21} = \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (y)$, $n_{22} = \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (x)$. The diagonal entries of $E_{\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_{\alpha}}}(n)$ are $\frac{1}{2}(x + \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (\Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (x))) = x$. For the $(1,2)$ entry, we first calculate the coefficient $b$ before the phase shift
     $$b = \frac{1}{2}\left( e^{i(\alpha-\beta)}y + e^{i(\beta-\alpha)}\Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (\Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (y)) \right) = y \left( \frac{e^{i(\alpha-\beta)} + e^{-i(\alpha-\beta)}}{2} \right) = y \cos(\beta-\alpha).$$
     Applying the structural phase shift for $\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_{\alpha}}$, the projection becomes
     $$E_{\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_{\alpha}}}(n) = \begin{bmatrix} x & y \cos(\beta-\alpha) e^{i(\beta-\alpha)} \\ \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (y) \cos(\beta-\alpha) e^{i(\alpha-\beta)} & \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (x) \end{bmatrix}.$$
     
      Subtracting the projection $E_{\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\alpha}}(n)$ from $n$, we get 
     $$w = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & y - y \cos(\beta-\alpha) e^{i(\beta-\alpha)} \\ \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (y) - \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (y) \cos(\beta-\alpha) e^{i(\alpha-\beta)} & 0 \end{bmatrix}.$$
     We can simplify the $(1,2)$ entry by expressing $\cos(\beta-\alpha)$ in terms of complex exponentials or using Euler's formula directly. Letting $\gamma = \beta - \alpha$, we have
     $$1 - \cos(\gamma)e^{i\gamma} = 1 - \cos(\gamma)(\cos(\gamma) + i\sin(\gamma)) = 1 - \cos^2(\gamma) - i\sin(\gamma)\cos(\gamma)$$$$= \sin^2(\gamma) - i\sin(\gamma)\cos(\gamma) = -i\sin(\gamma)(\cos(\gamma) + i\sin(\gamma)) = -i\sin(\gamma)e^{i\gamma}.$$
     A similar simplification for the $(2,1)$ entry yields $i\sin(\gamma)e^{-i\gamma}$. Thus,:
     $$w = \sin(\beta-\alpha) \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -i y e^{i(\beta-\alpha)} \\ i \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (y) e^{i(\alpha-\beta)} & 0 \end{bmatrix}.$$
     
     Now we get,
     $$w^* w = \sin^2(\beta-\alpha) \begin{bmatrix} \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (y^*) \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (y) & 0 \\ 0 & y^* y \end{bmatrix} = \sin^2(\beta-\alpha) \begin{bmatrix} \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (y^* y) & 0 \\ 0 & y^* y \end{bmatrix}.$$
     Applying the trace on $
  \mathbb{M}_{2}\IfValueT{\otimes}{(\otimes)}
 \mathscr{R}$
     $$\tau(w^* w) = \frac{1}{2} \left[ \tau_\mathscr{R}(\sin^2(\beta-\alpha) \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (y^* y)) + \tau_\mathscr{R}(\sin^2(\beta-\alpha) y^* y) \right].$$
     Since $\Theta_{\alpha, \beta} $ is trace-preserving, this gives the $\tau$-norm distance for an arbitrary $n$
     $$\Vert{}\eta(n) - \eta(E_{\mathscr{R}_u}(n))\Vert{}_\tau = \vert{}\sin(\beta-\alpha)\vert{} \Vert{}y\Vert{}_{\tau_\mathscr{R}}.$$
     
      As  $n \in \left( \mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_{\beta}}\right)_1$, the operator norm bound $\Vert{}n\Vert{} \le 1$ implies that the $(2,2)$ entry of $n^*n$ satisfies
     $$y^*y + \Theta_{\alpha, \beta} (x^*x) \le 1_\mathscr{R}.$$
     Taking the trace $\tau_\mathscr{R}$ yields $\Vert{}y\Vert{}_{\tau_\mathscr{R}}^2 + \Vert{}x\Vert{}_{\tau_\mathscr{R}}^2 \le 1$, meaning $\Vert{}y\Vert{}_{\tau_\mathscr{R}} \le 1$. Therefore, the distance is bounded above by $\vert{}\sin(\beta-\alpha)\vert{}$. To confirm the supremum is attained, we can choose the specific element $n_0 \in \mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_{\beta}}$ by setting $x = 0$ and $y = 1_\mathscr{R}$ 
     $$n_0 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1_\mathscr{R} \\ 1_\mathscr{R} & 0 \end{bmatrix}.$$
    Since, $n_0^* n_0 = 1_{
  \mathbb{M}_{2}\IfValueT{\otimes}{(\otimes)}
 \mathscr{R}}$, we have,  $\Vert{}n_0\Vert{} = 1$ and it lies in the $\left( \mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_{\beta}}\right)_1$. Thus, we get 
    $$\Vert{}\eta(n_0) - \eta(E_{\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_{\alpha}}}(n_0))\Vert{}_\tau = \vert{}\sin(\beta-\alpha)\vert{} \Vert{}1_\mathscr{R}\Vert{}_{\tau_\mathscr{R}} = \vert{}\sin(\beta-\alpha)\vert{}.$$
    Therefore, the supremum is exact
    $$\sup_{n\in \left( \mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_{\beta}}\right)_1} \Vert{}\eta(n) - \eta(E_{\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_{\alpha}}}(n))\Vert{}_\tau = \vert{}\sin(\beta-\alpha)\vert{}.$$
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:mt-distance-2by2}
 For two distinct $\alpha,\beta\in[0,\pi)$, we have
  \[
  \mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{MT}}(\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_{\alpha}}, \mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_{\beta}})= \vert{}\sin(\alpha-\beta)\vert{}.
\]
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
The proof follows from Lemma \ref{lem:one-sided-spin}, Lemma \ref{lem:other-sided-spin} and Theorem \ref{thm:mashood_taylor}.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- cor-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:dmt-is-continuous}
    For every $r \in [0,1]$, there exists $2\times2$ Hadamard unitaries $u$ and $v$ such that
    \[
    \mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{MT}}(\mathscr{R}_u,\mathscr{R}_v)=r.
    \]
<!-- end cor-1 -->
<!-- cor-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:dmt-is-same-alpha-2by2}
   For two distinct $\alpha,\beta\in[0,\pi)$, we have
\[
\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{MT}}(\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_{\alpha}}, \mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_{\beta}})
=
\sqrt{1-\operatorname{cos}\left(\alpha_{\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_{\alpha}}\cap \mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_{\beta}}}^{\mathscr{R}}(\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_{\alpha}},\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_{\beta}})\right)}.
\]
<!-- end cor-2 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
The proof follows from the Theorem \ref{thm:mt-distance-2by2} and \cite[Theorem 5.10]{BG2025-1}.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- cor-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:angle-not-quantized}
    For every $\theta  \in [0,\frac{\pi}{2}]$, there exist $\alpha, \beta \in [0, \pi)$ such that
    \[
    \alpha^\mathscr{R}_{\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\alpha} \cap \mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\beta}}(\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\alpha},\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\beta})=\theta .
    \]
<!-- end cor-3 -->
<!-- cor-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:comm-sq-d-1-2times2}
   Let $\alpha,\beta\in[0,\pi)$ be distinct. Then the following quadruple
    \[
\begin{array}{ccc}
\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\alpha}  & \subset & \mathscr{R} \\
\cup && \cup \\
\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\alpha} \cap \mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\beta} & \subset & \mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\beta}
\end{array}
\]
is a commuting square if and only if $\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{MT}} (\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\alpha}, \mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\beta}) = 1.$
<!-- end cor-4 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
This follows immediately from Corollary \ref{cor:dmt-is-same-alpha-2by2} and \cite[Proposition 2.4]{bakshi-etal-2019}.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- cor-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:comm-sq-dkk-1-2times2}
   Let $\alpha,\beta\in[0,\pi)$ be distinct. If the following quadruple is a commuting square
    \[
\begin{array}{ccc}
\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\alpha}  & \subset & \mathscr{R} \\
\cup && \cup \\
\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\alpha} \cap \mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\beta} & \subset & \mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\beta}
\end{array}
\]
then $\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{KK}} (\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\alpha}, \mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_\beta}) = 1.$
<!-- end cor-5 -->
<!-- lem-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:circle}
    Let $X = [0, \pi)$ and define $d: X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ by $d(\alpha, \beta) = \vert{}\sin(\alpha - \beta)\vert{}$. Then $(X, d)$ is a compact metric space that is isometric to a circle of radius $1/2$ equipped with the Euclidean chordal metric.
<!-- end lem-9 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Consider the mapping $f: X \to \mathbb{C}$ defined by $f(\theta) = \frac{1}{2}e^{2i\theta}$. The map $f$ is a bijection from $X$ onto the circle of radius $1/2$ centered at the origin, denoted $C_{1/2}$.
    
    Then any two points $\alpha, \beta \in X$:
    $$
    \vert{}f(\alpha) - f(\beta)\vert{} = \frac{1}{2} \vert{}e^{2i\alpha} - e^{2i\beta}\vert{}
    =\frac{1}{2} \left\vert{} e^{i(\alpha+\beta)} (e^{i(\alpha-\beta)} - e^{-i(\alpha-\beta)}) \right\vert{}
    = \vert{}\sin(\alpha - \beta)\vert{} = d(\alpha, \beta)
    $$
    Therefore $f$ is an isometry between $(X, d)$ and $(C_{1/2}, \vert{}\cdot\vert{})$.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:sp-2-is-circle}
    The space $\mathrm{Sp}_2$ of all $2\times2$ spin model subfactors, equipped with the metric $\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{MT}}$, is homeomorphic to the circle group $\mathbb{T}$:
\[
(\mathrm{Sp}_2,\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{MT}})\cong \mathbb{T}.
\]
In particular, $(\mathrm{Sp}_2,\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{MT}})$ is a compact and path connected metric space.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:H2-bg-is-circle}
The quotient space $
  \mathbb{H}^u_{2}\IfValueT{/}{(/)}
\sim$, equipped with the product $\odot_{\mathrm{sp}}$, is an abelian group. Moreover,
\[
\bigl(
  \mathbb{H}^u_{2}\IfValueT{/}{(/)}
\sim,\odot_{\mathrm{sp}}\bigr)
\cong \mathbb{T}.
\]
In particular, $
  \mathbb{H}^u_{2}\IfValueT{/}{(/)}
\sim$ is a compact, connected abelian topological group.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
The operation $\boxplus$ also induces a group structure on the chosen family of representatives
\[
\mathcal{H}_2^{\mathrm{sp}}
:=
\{\mathsf{H}_\alpha:\alpha\in[0,\pi)\}.
\]
More precisely, defining
\[
\mathsf{H}_\alpha\odot_{\mathrm{sp}}\mathsf{H}_\beta
:=
\mathsf{H}_{\alpha\boxplus\beta},
\qquad
\alpha,\beta\in[0,\pi),
\]
endows $\mathcal{H}_2^{\mathrm{sp}}$ with an abelian group structure. The map
\[
\mathsf{H}_\alpha
\longmapsto
e^{2i\alpha}
\]
is then a group isomorphism from $(\mathcal{H}_2^{\mathrm{sp}},\odot_{\mathrm{sp}})$ onto the circle group $\mathbb{T}$. Thus, the same circle-group structure appears naturally at three levels: on the parameter space $[0,\pi)$ equipped with $\boxplus$, on the quotient $
  \mathbb{H}^u_{2}\IfValueT{/}{(/)}
\sim$, and on the corresponding family of representatives of $2\times2$ Hadamard unitaries.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- prop-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:uni-reg-spin}
    Let $u$ be an $n\times n$ Hadamard unitary in $
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{$}{($)}
 such that
    $u\sim_{\mathrm{h}}\mathsf{F}_{n}$. Then $\mathscr{R}_u\subseteq\mathscr{R}$ is unitary regular.
<!-- end prop-7 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Since $u\sim_{\mathrm{h}}\mathsf{F}_{n}$, it follows from \cite[Theorem 5.2]{BGG-2025}
that $\mathscr{R}_u$ and $\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{F}_{n}}$ are isomorphic. On the other hand,
it is readily verified that
\[
\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{F}_{n}}\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_n\cong\mathscr{R}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
(\mathscr{R}_u\subseteq\mathscr{R})
\cong
(\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{F}_{n}}\subseteq\mathscr{R})
\cong
(\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{F}_{n}}\subseteq
\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{F}_{n}}\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_n),
\]
and the latter inclusion is unitary regular. Hence, $\mathscr{R}_u\subseteq\mathscr{R}$
is unitary regular.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- lem-10: body_md -->
\label{lem:uncountable-unitaries}
    For any integer $n \ge 2$, there exists an uncountable family of Hadamard unitaries $\{ u_\lambda \}_{\lambda \in I}$ in $
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{$}{($)}
 such that:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item[(i)] $u_\lambda \sim_{\mathrm{h}} \mathsf{F}_{n}$ for all $\lambda \in I$.
        \item[(ii)] $u_\lambda \not\sim \mathsf{F}_{n}$ for all $\lambda \in I$.
        \item[(iii)] $u_\lambda \not\sim u_\mu$ for all $\lambda \neq \mu$ in $I$.
    \end{itemize}
<!-- end lem-10 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Let $\Omega_n = \{ 1, \omega, \omega^2, \dots, \omega^{n-1} \}$ denote the set of $n$-th roots of unity.
    
    Define the index set $I$ to be the open arc on the unit circle given by:
    $$I := \{ e^{i\theta} \mid 0 < \theta < 2\pi/n \}$$
    Note that $I$ contains no $n$-th roots of unity.

    For each $\lambda \in I$, define the diagonal unitary matrix $D_\lambda = \operatorname{diag}(1, \lambda, 1, \dots, 1)$ and construct the Hadamard unitary:
    $$u_\lambda = D_\lambda \mathsf{F}_{n}.$$
    Since $\mathsf{F}_{n}$ is a Hadamard unitary and $u_\lambda$ is obtained from $\mathsf{F}_{n}$ by left-multiplying by a diagonal unitary matrix, $u_\lambda$ is also a Hadamard unitary. By definition of Hadamard equivalence, this immediately establishes that $u_\lambda \sim_{\mathrm{h}} \mathsf{F}_{n}$ for all $\lambda \in I$, proving property $(i)$.



    To prove property $(ii)$, assume for the sake of contradiction that $u_\lambda \sim \mathsf{F}_{n}$ for some $\lambda \in I$. By the definition of Bakshi--Guin equivalence, there exist an $n \times n$ permutation matrix $P$ and a diagonal unitary matrix $D = \operatorname{diag}(d_0, d_1, \dots, d_{n-1})$ such that
    $$u_\lambda = \mathsf{F}_{n} P D.$$


    Substitute $u_\lambda = D_\lambda \mathsf{F}_{n}$. The $(0,0)$-entry of $D_\lambda$ is $1$, so the $0$-th row of $u_\lambda$ is identical to the $0$-th row of $\mathsf{F}_{n}$, which is $\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}(1, 1, \dots, 1)$. On the right side, multiplying $\mathsf{F}_{n}$ by the permutation matrix $P$ leaves the uniform $0$-th row unchanged. Multiplying by $D$ scales the $k$-th entry of the $0$-th row by $d_k$. Equating the $0$-th rows of both sides gives
    $$\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}(1, 1, \dots, 1) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}(d_0, d_1, \dots, d_{n-1}).$$
    This implies $d_k = 1$ for all $k$, so $D$ is the identity matrix $\mathbb{I}_n$. The equation reduces to $u_\lambda = \mathsf{F}_{n} P$.

    Now compare the $1$-st row of both sides. The $1$-st row of $u_\lambda = D_\lambda \mathsf{F}_{n}$ is multiplied by $\lambda$, so its entries form the set $\{ \frac{\lambda}{\sqrt{n}}\omega^k \mid 0 \le k \le n-1 \}$. The $1$-st row of $\mathsf{F}_{n} P$ is a permutation of the $1$-st row of $\mathsf{F}_{n}$, so its entries form the set $\{ \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\omega^k \mid 0 \le k \le n-1 \}$. Since $u_\lambda = \mathsf{F}_{n} P$, these two sets of entries must be equal. However, this requires $\lambda = \omega^k$ for some integer $k$, which implies $\lambda \in \Omega_n$. This contradicts our construction that $I \cap \Omega_n = \varnothing$. Thus, $u_\lambda \not\sim \mathsf{F}_{n}$ for all $\lambda \in I$, proving property $(ii)$.

    To prove property $(iii)$, suppose that $u_\lambda \sim u_\mu$ for some $\lambda, \mu \in I$. By definition, there exist a permutation matrix $P$ and a diagonal unitary matrix $D = \operatorname{diag}(d_0, d_1, \dots, d_{n-1})$ such that:
    $$u_\lambda = u_\mu P D$$

    Substitute the definitions of $u_\lambda$ and $u_\mu$:

    $$D_\lambda \mathsf{F}_{n} = D_\mu \mathsf{F}_{n} P D$$

    Consider the $0$-th row of both sides. Since the $(0,0)$-entries of both $D_\lambda$ and $D_\mu$ are $1$, the $0$-th rows of $D_\lambda \mathsf{F}_{n}$ and $D_\mu \mathsf{F}_{n}$ are both precisely $\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}(1, 1, \dots, 1)$. Right-multiplying $D_\mu \mathsf{F}_{n}$ by $P$ leaves this uniform row unchanged, and right-multiplying by $D$ scales the $k$-th entry by $d_k$. Equating the $0$-th rows of both sides yields:

    $$\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}(1, 1, \dots, 1) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}(d_0, d_1, \dots, d_{n-1})$$

    This forces $d_k = 1$ for all $k$, so $D = \mathbb{I}_n$. The equivalence simplifies to
    $$u_\lambda = u_\mu P.$$

    Now, consider the $1$-st row of this simplified equation. The $1$-st row of $u_\lambda$ consists of the entries $\frac{\lambda}{\sqrt{n}}\omega^k$ for $0 \le k \le n-1$. The $1$-st row of $u_\mu P$ is a permutation of the $1$-st row of $u_\mu$, which consists of the entries $\frac{\mu}{\sqrt{n}}\omega^k$ for $0 \le k \le n-1$. Because $u_\lambda = u_\mu P$, the sets of entries in their $1$-st rows must be identical

    $$\left\{ \frac{\lambda}{\sqrt{n}} \omega^k \;\middle\vert{}\; 0 \le k \le n-1 \right\} = \left\{ \frac{\mu}{\sqrt{n}} \omega^k \;\middle\vert{}\; 0 \le k \le n-1 \right\}.$$

    This set equality requires that the specific element $\frac{\lambda}{\sqrt{n}} \cdot 1$ from the left set must equal some element in the right set. Thus, there exists an integer $k$ ($0 \le k \le n-1$) such that

    $$\lambda = \mu \omega^k \implies \lambda \mu^{-1} = \omega^k.$$

    Since $\lambda, \mu \in I$, we can write $\lambda = e^{i\theta_1}$ and $\mu = e^{i\theta_2}$ for some angles $\theta_1, \theta_2 \in (0, 2\pi/n)$. The ratio $\lambda \mu^{-1} = e^{i(\theta_1 - \theta_2)}$ has an argument $\theta_1 - \theta_2$ that strictly satisfies:

    $$-\frac{2\pi}{n} < \theta_1 - \theta_2 < \frac{2\pi}{n}.$$

    The only $n$-th root of unity $\omega^k = e^{2\pi i k / n}$ whose argument falls strictly within the open interval $(-2\pi/n, 2\pi/n)$ is $\omega^0 = 1$.

    Therefore, we must have $\lambda \mu^{-1} = 1$, which implies $\lambda = \mu$. By contraposition, if $\lambda \neq \mu$ in $I$, then $u_\lambda \not\sim u_\mu$. This establishes property $(iii)$ and completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- prop-8: body_md -->
\label{prop:uncountable-reg-spin-models}
    For each $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the hyperfinite $\mathrm{II}_1$-factor $\mathscr{R}$ contains an uncountable family of pairwise distinct regular $n \times n$ spin model subfactors.
<!-- end prop-8 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{U}$ be an uncountable family of Hadamard unitaries in $
  \mathbb{M}_{n}\IfValueT{$}{($)}
 as provided by Lemma \ref{lem:uncountable-unitaries}. By condition~(iii) of the lemma and \cite[Theorem 4.7]{BG2025-1}, the spin model subfactors associated with the unitaries in $\mathcal{U}$ are pairwise distinct. On the other hand, condition~(i) ensures that every $u \in \mathcal{U}$ is Hadamard equivalent to $\mathsf{F}_{n}$. Therefore, Proposition \ref{prop:uni-reg-spin} implies that each of the corresponding spin model subfactors is regular. Hence, $\mathcal{U}$ gives rise to an uncountable family of pairwise distinct regular $n \times n$ Spin model subfactors of $\mathscr{R}$.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
\label{rem:comm-sq-vs-max-d}
The phenomenon observed in Corollary \ref{cor:comm-sq-d-1-2times2} and \ref{cor:comm-sq-dkk-1-2times2} does not hold for a general inclusion of $\mathrm{II}_1$ factors $\mathcal N \subseteq \mathcal M$. In particular, two intermediate subfactors may attain the maximal Kadison--Kastler distance without forming a commuting square. We illustrate this with the following example.

Let $G$ be a finite group acting outerly on the hyperfinite $\mathrm{II}_1$-factor $\mathscr{R}$, and let $H,K$ be two non-trivial distinct subgroups of $G$ such that $H \cap K \ne \{e \}$. Then it is well known that the following quadruple is not a commuting square:
\[ \begin{array}{ccc} \mathscr{R} \rtimes H & \subset & \mathscr{R} \rtimes G \\ \cup && \cup \\ \mathscr{R} & \subset & \mathscr{R} \rtimes K \end{array} \]
Hence,
\[
\alpha(\mathscr{R}\rtimes H,\mathscr{R}\rtimes K)\neq \frac{\pi}{2},
\]
and consequently, by \cite[Proposition 2.4]{bakshi-etal-2019}, the above square is not a commuting square. On the other hand, \cite[Theorem 5.11]{kumar-2026} implies that
\[
\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{MT}}(\mathscr{R}\rtimes H,\mathscr{R}\rtimes K)
=
1
=
\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{KK}}(\mathscr{R}\rtimes H,\mathscr{R}\rtimes K).
\]
Thus, the two intermediate subfactors are at maximal Kadison--Kastler distance even though they do not form a commuting square.

For the converse direction, namely, whether the formation of a commuting square forces the Kadison--Kastler distance to be maximal, we provide a sufficient condition in Theorem \ref{thm:comm-sq-imply-d-1-ii-1}.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- prop-9: body_md -->
\label{prop:exist-exp-zero-uni}
    Let $\mathcal{N} \subseteq \mathcal{M}$ be an inclusion of $\mathrm{II}_1$-subfactors with $[\mathcal{M}:\mathcal{N}] \in \{2,3\} \cup [4,\infty]$. Then there exists a unitary $u \in \mathcal{M}$ such that $E_{\mathcal{N}}(u) = 0$ where $E_\mathcal N$ be the canonical trace preserving conditional expectation onto $\mathcal N$.
<!-- end prop-9 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
Following Popa \cite{popa-1989-rel-dim}, we define the set of relative dimensions $\Lambda(\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{N})$ as the set of all scalars $\alpha \in [0, 1]$ for which there exists a projection $p \in \mathcal{M}$ such that $E_{\mathcal{N}}(p) = \alpha 1_{\mathcal{N}}$. 
    
    If we can show that $1/2 \in \Lambda(\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{N})$, then there exists a projection $p \in \mathcal{M}$ satisfying $E_{\mathcal{N}}(p) = \frac{1}{2} 1_{\mathcal{N}}$. We can then define the element $u = 2p - 1$. Because $p$ is a projection, $u$ is a self-adjoint unitary in $\mathcal{M}$. Applying the conditional expectation yields
    $$E_{\mathcal{N}}(u) = 2 E_{\mathcal{N}}(p) - 1_{\mathcal{N}} = 2\left(\frac{1}{2} 1_{\mathcal{N}}\right) - 1_{\mathcal{N}} = 0,$$
    which would complete the proof. Thus, it suffices to prove that $1/2 \in \Lambda(\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{N})$ for all index values in the given range. Let $\lambda = [\mathcal{M}:\mathcal{N}]^{-1}$.

    \textbf{Case 1:} Assume $[\mathcal{M}:\mathcal{N}] \in [4, \infty]$. 
    By Theorem 5.2 of \cite{popa-1989-rel-dim}, setting the parameter $t = 1/2$ directly implies that $1/2 \in \Lambda(\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{N})$ for any subfactor with index greater than or equal to $4$.

    \textbf{Case 2:} Assume $[\mathcal{M}:\mathcal{N}] \in \{2, 3\}$.
    By the index rigidity theorem, these values correspond to the discrete part of the Jones spectrum, where the index takes the form $4\cos^2(\pi/n)$ for $n=4$ and $n=6$, respectively. By Theorem 5.1 of \cite{popa-1989-rel-dim}, the set of relative dimensions for this discrete spectrum is explicitly given by:
    $$\Lambda(\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{N}) = \{0\} \cup \left\{ \lambda \frac{P_{k-1}(\lambda)}{P_k(\lambda)} \;\middle|\; 1 \le k \le n-2 \right\},$$
    where $P_k(x)$ are polynomials defined recursively by $P_0(x) = 1$, $P_1(x) = 1$, and $P_{k+1}(x) = P_k(x) - x P_{k-1}(x)$.
    \begin{itemize}
        \item For $[\mathcal{M}:\mathcal{N}] = 2$ (which means $n=4$ and $\lambda = 1/2$), evaluating the polynomials for $k=1, 2$ explicitly yields $\Lambda(\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{N}) = \{0, 1/2, 1\}$. Clearly, $1/2 \in \Lambda(\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{N})$.
        \item For $[\mathcal{M}:\mathcal{N}] = 3$ (which means $n=6$ and $\lambda = 1/3$), evaluating the polynomials up to $k=4$ yields the set of relative dimensions $\{0, 1/3, 1/2, 2/3, 1\}$. Again, $1/2 \in \Lambda(\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{N})$.
    \end{itemize}

    In all cases, we have established that $1/2 \in \Lambda(\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{N})$. The existence of the trace-zero unitary $u = 2p - 1$ immediately follows.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:dkk-is-1-for-comm-sq-spin}
Let $\mathcal M$ be a finite von Neumann algebra, and let $\mathcal N,\mathcal P,\mathcal Q$ be $\mathrm{II}_1$-subfactors of $\mathcal M$ such that
\[
\begin{array}{ccc}
    \mathcal P & \subset & \mathcal M \\
    \cup && \cup \\
    \mathcal N & \subset & \mathcal Q
\end{array}
\]
is a commuting square. Suppose that the index of at least one of the inclusions $\mathcal N\subseteq\mathcal P$ or $\mathcal N\subseteq\mathcal Q$ belongs to $\{2,3\}\cup[4,\infty]$. Then $\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{KK}}(\mathcal P,\mathcal Q)=1=\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{MT}}(\mathcal P,\mathcal Q)$.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
Without loss of generality, assume that $[\mathcal P: \mathcal N]\in \{2,3\}\cup [4, \infty]$. 
Let $E^{\mathcal M}_{\mathcal N}: \mathcal M \to \mathcal N$, $E^{\mathcal M}_{\mathcal P}: \mathcal M \to \mathcal P$ and $E^{\mathcal P}_{\mathcal N}: \mathcal P \to \mathcal N$ be the unique trace-preserving conditional expectations. Then, for any $x\in \mathcal M$, we have
\[
E^{\mathcal P}_{\mathcal N} \circ E^{\mathcal M}_{\mathcal P}(x) = E^{\mathcal M}_{\mathcal N}(x).
\]
Let $x\in \left( P\right)_1$. Then
\[
\|\eta(x)-\eta(E^{\mathcal M}_{\mathcal Q}(x))\|^2_{\tau}
= \|\eta(x)-\eta(E^{\mathcal M}_{\mathcal Q}(E^{\mathcal M}_{\mathcal P}(x)))\|^2_{\tau}
= \|\eta(x-E^{\mathcal M}_{\mathcal N}(x))\|^2_{\tau}
= \|\eta(x)\|^2_{\tau}-\|\eta(E^{\mathcal M}_{\mathcal N}(x))\|^2_{\tau}
\leq 1.
\]
This implies that
\[
\sup_{x \in \left( P\right)_1}\|\eta(x)-\eta(E^{\mathcal M}_{\mathcal Q}(x))\|_{\tau}\leq 1.
\]

Now, by Proposition \ref{prop:exist-exp-zero-uni}, there exists a unitary $u\in \mathcal P$ such that $E^{\mathcal P}_{\mathcal N}(u)=0$. Hence,
\[
\|\eta(u)-\eta(E^{\mathcal M}_{\mathcal Q}(u))\|^2_{\tau}
= \|\eta(u)\|^2_{\tau}-\|\eta(E^{\mathcal M}_{\mathcal N}(u))\|^2_{\tau}
= \|\eta(u)\|^2_{\tau}-\|\eta(E^{\mathcal P}_{\mathcal N}\circ E^{\mathcal M}_{\mathcal P}(u))\|^2_{\tau}
=1.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\sup_{x \in \left( P\right)_1}\|\eta(x)-\eta(E^{\mathcal M}_{\mathcal Q}(x))\|_{\tau}=1.
\]
The result now follows from Theorem \ref{thm:mashood_taylor} and Proposition \ref{prop:mt_and_kk}.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:comm-sq-imply-d-1-ii-1}
    Let $\mathcal N \subseteq \mathcal M$ be $\mathrm{II}_1$ subfactors with $[\mathcal{M}:\mathcal{N}]\ge 4$, and let $\mathcal P,\mathcal Q$ be intermediate $\mathrm{II}_1$ subfactors.
    Suppose that
    \[
        \begin{array}{ccc}
            \mathcal P & \subset & \mathcal M \\
            \cup & & \cup \\
            \mathcal N & \subset & \mathcal Q
        \end{array}
    \]
    is a commuting square. Then
    \[
        \mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{MT}}(\mathcal P,\mathcal Q)=1=\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{KK}}(\mathcal P,\mathcal Q).
    \]
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
Let $E^{\mathcal M}_{\mathcal N}: \mathcal M \to \mathcal N$, $E^{\mathcal M}_{\mathcal P}: \mathcal M \to \mathcal P$ and $E^{\mathcal P}_{\mathcal N}: \mathcal P \to \mathcal N$ be the unique trace-preserving conditional expectations. Then, for any $x\in \mathcal M$, we have
\[
E^{\mathcal P}_{\mathcal N} \circ E^{\mathcal M}_{\mathcal P}(x) = E^{\mathcal M}_{\mathcal N}(x).
\]
Let $x\in \left( P\right)_1$. Then
\[
\|\eta(x)-\eta(E^{\mathcal M}_{\mathcal Q}(x))\|^2_{\tau}
= \|\eta(x)-\eta(E^{\mathcal M}_{\mathcal Q}(E^{\mathcal M}_{\mathcal P}(x)))\|^2_{\tau}
= \|\eta(x-E^{\mathcal M}_{\mathcal N}(x))\|^2_{\tau}
= \|\eta(x)\|^2_{\tau}-\|\eta(E^{\mathcal M}_{\mathcal N}(x))\|^2_{\tau}
\leq 1.
\]
This implies that
\[
\sup_{x \in \left( P\right)_1}\|\eta(x)-\eta(E^{\mathcal M}_{\mathcal Q}(x))\|_{\tau}\leq 1.
\]

Now, by Proposition \ref{prop:exist-exp-zero-uni}, there exists a unitary $u\in \mathcal P$ such that $E^{\mathcal P}_{\mathcal N}(u)=0$. Hence,
\[
\|\eta(u)-\eta(E^{\mathcal M}_{\mathcal Q}(u))\|^2_{\tau}
= \|\eta(u)\|^2_{\tau}-\|\eta(E^{\mathcal M}_{\mathcal N}(u))\|^2_{\tau}
= \|\eta(u)\|^2_{\tau}-\|\eta(E^{\mathcal P}_{\mathcal N}\circ E^{\mathcal M}_{\mathcal P}(u))\|^2_{\tau}
=1.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\sup_{x \in \left( P\right)_1}\|\eta(x)-\eta(E^{\mathcal M}_{\mathcal Q}(x))\|_{\tau}=1.
\]
The result now follows from Theorem \ref{thm:mashood_taylor} and Proposition \ref{prop:mt_and_kk}.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{thm:spin-model-n-times-n}
    Let $u,v\in
  \mathbb{H}^u_{n}\IfValueT{$}{($)}
 with $u\not\sim v$ such that $\mathscr{R}_u\cap\mathscr{R}_v$ is a finite-index subfactor of $\mathscr{R}$.
    If
    \[
        \begin{array}{ccc}
            \mathscr{R}_u & \subset & \mathscr{R} \\
            \cup && \cup \\
            \mathscr{R}_u\cap\mathscr{R}_v & \subset & \mathscr{R}_v
        \end{array}
    \]
    is a commuting square, then
    \[
        \mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{KK}}(\mathscr{R}_u,\mathscr{R}_v)=1=\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{MT}}(\mathscr{R}_u, \mathscr{R}_v).
    \]
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
We have

    \[
    [\mathscr{R}:\mathscr{R}_u\cap\mathscr{R}_v]=\begin{cases}
        4 &\text{ if } n = 2\\
       9 &\text{ if } n = 3\\
       \ge 4 & \text{ if } n \ge 4.
    \end{cases}
    \]
    The conclusion now follows immediately from Theorem~\ref{thm:comm-sq-imply-d-1-ii-1}.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- cor-6: body_md -->
\label{cor:necessity-for-commuting-square}
Let $u,v\in
  \mathbb{H}^u_{n}\IfValueT{$}{($)}
 with $u\not\sim v$ and $\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{KK}}(\mathscr{R}_u,\mathscr{R}_v)\ne 1$. Then either $\mathscr{R}_u\cap\mathscr{R}_v$ is not a finite-index subfactor of $\mathscr{R}$, or the quadruple $(\mathscr{R},\mathscr{R}_u,\mathscr{R}_v,\mathscr{R}_u\cap\mathscr{R}_v)$ does not form a commuting square.
<!-- end cor-6 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal M$ be a finite von Neumann algebra with a faithful normal tracial state $\tau$, and let $\mathcal B_1,\mathcal B_2$ be von Neumann subalgebras of $\mathcal M$. We say that $\mathcal B_1$ is orthogonal to $\mathcal B_2$ if $\tau(b_1b_2)=0$ whenever $b_1\in \mathcal B_1$ and $b_2\in \mathcal B_2$ satisfy $\tau(b_1)=\tau(b_2)=0$.
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\label{rem:popa-ortho-not-same}
    Note that, by \cite[Lemma 2.1]{popa-1983}, if $\mathcal P$ and $\mathcal Q$ are orthogonal in $\mathcal M$ in the sense of Popa, then $\mathcal P \cap \mathcal Q = \mathbb{C}$ and $(\mathbb{C},\mathcal P,\mathcal Q,\mathcal M)$ forms a commuting square. On the other hand, by \cite{BG2025-1}, the intersection $\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_{\alpha}} \cap \mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_{\beta}}$ is a $\mathrm{II}_1$ subfactor and, in particular, can never be equal to $\mathbb{C}$. Thus, for any $\alpha,\beta \in [0,\pi)$, the Spin model subfactors $\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_{\alpha}}$ and $\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_{\beta}}$ can never be orthogonal inside the hyperfinite $\mathrm{II}_1$-factor in the sense of Popa.

On the other hand, Corollary~\ref{cor:dmt-is-same-alpha-2by2} shows that whenever the distance between $\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_{\alpha}}$ and $\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_{\beta}}$ is maximal, their interior angle over their intersection is maximal, namely,
\[
\alpha_{\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_{\alpha}} \cap \mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_{\beta}}}^\mathscr{R}
\bigl(\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_{\alpha}},\mathscr{R}_{\mathsf{H}_{\beta}}\bigr)
= \frac{\pi}{2}.
\]
Thus, orthogonality in terms of the interior angle is distinct from, and does not imply, orthogonality in the sense of Popa.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{thm:diffuse-comm-sq}
Let $(\mathcal M, \tau)$ be a finite von Neumann algebra, and let $\mathcal P,\mathcal Q\subseteq \mathcal M$ be diffuse orthogonal subalgebras. Then
\[
\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{KK}}(\mathcal P,\mathcal Q)=1=\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{MT}}(\mathcal P,\mathcal Q).
\]
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
Since $\mathcal P$ and $\mathcal Q$ are orthogonal then by Lemma 2.1-((i) $\implies$ (iv)) of \cite{popa-1983}, we get $E_\mathcal Q E_\mathcal P = \tau(-) 1_\mathcal M$. Therefore, for any $x \in \mathcal P$, applying $E_\mathcal Q$ yields:
    $$E_\mathcal Q(x) = E_\mathcal Q(E_\mathcal P(x)) =  \tau(x)1_\mathcal M$$
    
    Because $\mathcal P$ is a diffuse von Neumann algebra, it contains a Haar unitary $u$. This unitary satisfies $u \in \left( \mathcal P\right)_1$, $\Vert{}u\Vert{}_\tau = 1$, and $\tau(u) = 0$. 
    
    Then, we get 
    $$\Vert{}\eta(u - E_\mathcal Q(u))\Vert{}_\tau = \Vert{}\eta(u - \tau(u)1)\Vert{}_\tau = \Vert{}\eta(u - 0)\Vert{}_\tau = 1.$$
    
    Since the supremum over $\left( \mathcal P\right)_1$ cannot exceed $1$ (as $\Vert{}\eta(x - E_\mathcal Q(x))\Vert{}_\tau \le \Vert{}\eta(x)\Vert{}_\tau \le 1$), we immediately obtain
    $$\sup_{x \in \left( \mathcal P\right)_1} \Vert{}\eta(x - E_\mathcal Q(x))\Vert{}_\tau = 1.$$
    Then by Theorem \ref{thm:mashood_taylor} and Proposition \ref{prop:mt_and_kk}, we get 
    $$\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{KK}}(\mathcal P, \mathcal Q)= \mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{MT}}(\mathcal P, \mathcal Q) = 1.$$
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{exam:ortho-converse-not-true}
Let $\mathcal M = L^\infty(\mathbb{T}^3, \mu \times \mu \times \mu)$, where $\mathbb{T} = \mathbb{R} / 2\pi\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mu$ is the normalized Haar measure. We equip $\mathcal M$ with the standard tracial state $\tau$ given by integration over $\mathbb{T}^3$.

Define the following von Neumann subalgebras:
\begin{align*}
\mathcal P &= \{ f \in \mathcal M \mid f(r, s, t) = g(r, s) \text{ for some } g \in L^\infty(\mathbb{T}^2) \} \cong L^\infty(\mathbb{T}^2) \otimes 1,\\
\mathcal Q &= \{ f \in \mathcal M \mid f(r, s, t) = h(s, t) \text{ for some } h \in L^\infty(\mathbb{T}^2) \} \cong 1 \otimes L^\infty(\mathbb{T}^2).
\end{align*}
Both $\mathcal P$ and $\mathcal Q$ are diffuse, unital subalgebras of $\mathcal M$. We will show that $\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{MT}}(\mathcal P, \mathcal Q) = 1$, but $\mathcal P$ and $\mathcal Q$ are not orthogonal.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
Notice that $\mathcal P \cap \mathcal Q$ contains all functions that depend only on the middle variable $s$. 
Let $a(r,s,t) = \sqrt{2}\cos(s)$. Since $a$ depends only on $s$, we have $a \in \mathcal P$ and $a \in \mathcal Q$.

Then,
\[
\tau(a) = \int_{\mathbb{T}} \sqrt{2}\cos(s) \,d\mu(s) = 0.
\]
Therefore we have
\[
\tau(aa) = \tau(a^2) = \int_{\mathbb{T}} 2\cos^2(s) \,d\mu(s) = 1 \neq 0= \tau(a) \tau(a).
\]

\noindent\textbf{Claim: }$\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{MT}}(\mathcal P, \mathcal Q) = 1$.\\
Let $u(r,s,t) = e^{ir}$. Clearly, $u \in \mathcal P$ and $\|u\|_\infty = 1$, so $u \in \left( \mathcal P\right)_1$. Applying $E_\mathcal Q$, we get:
\[
E_\mathcal Q(u)(s,t) = \int_{\mathbb{T}} e^{ir} \,d\mu(r) = 0.
\]
Consequently, $\|u - E_\mathcal Q(u)\|_2 = \|u\|_2 = 1$.
Since $\|x - E_\mathcal Q(x)\|_2 \leq \|x\|_2 \leq 1$ for all $x \in \left( \mathcal P\right)_1$, we conclude that
\[
\sup_{x\in \left( \mathcal P\right)_1}\|\eta(x)-\eta(E_{\mathcal Q}(x))\|_{\tau} = 1.
\]

By symmetry, choosing $v(r,s,t) = e^{it} \in \left( \mathcal Q\right)_1$ yields $E_\mathcal P(v) = 0$ and $\|v - E_\mathcal P(v)\|_2 = 1$, which gives
\[
\sup_{z\in \left( \mathcal Q\right)_1}\|\eta(z)-\eta(E_{\mathcal P}(z))\|_{\tau} = 1.
\]

By Theorem \ref{thm:mashood_taylor}, we conclude that $\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{MT}}(\mathcal P, \mathcal Q)= 1$.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- lem-11: body_md -->
\label{lem:fourier_coeff}
    Let $G$ be a countable discrete group. Let $\Phi: \eta(L(G)) \to \ell^{2}(G)$
    be the linear isometry defined by
    \[
        \Phi(\eta(x)) := x\delta_e, \qquad x\in L(G).
    \]
    Then the following hold:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[(i)] $\Phi$ extends to a unitary operator from $L^2(L(G),\tau)$ onto $\ell^2(G)$. Consequently,
        \[
            \{\eta(\lambda_g):g\in G\}
        \]
        is an orthonormal basis for $L^2(L(G),\tau)$.

        \item[(ii)] For every $x\in L(G)$, the $g$-th Fourier coefficient $\langle \eta(x),\eta(\lambda_g)\rangle_{L^2}$ of $\eta(x)$ is equal to $\widehat{x}(g).$ Consequently,
        \begin{align*}
            \eta(x)
            = \sum_{g\in G}\widehat{x}(g)\eta(\lambda_g),\quad \text{ and }\quad
            \eta(x^*)
            = \sum_{g\in G}
            \overline{\widehat{x}(g)}
            \eta(\lambda_{g^{-1}}),
        \end{align*}
        where both series converge in the Hilbert space $L^2(L(G),\tau)$.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end lem-11 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
\noindent \textbf{(i).}  Since  the range of $\Phi$ is dense and it is isometry so it extends to an unitary from $L^2(L(G),\tau)$ onto $\ell^2(G)$.\\  
   \noindent \textbf{(ii).} First note that $\tau(\lambda_g^*x)$ is equal to the $g$-th Fourier coefficient of $x\delta_e$ for any $x \in L(G)$. Indeed,
   \[
   \langle x\delta_e, \delta_g \rangle_{\ell^2}= \langle x\delta_e, \lambda_g \delta_e \rangle_{\ell^2}=\langle \lambda_g^* x \delta_e, \delta_e \rangle_{\ell^2}= \tau(\lambda_g^* x).
   \]
   Hence we get
   \begin{align*}
       \widehat{x} = \Phi^{-1} (x\delta_e) = \Phi^{-1} \left( \sum_{g\in G} \tau(\lambda_g^* x) \delta_g   \right) = \sum_{g\in G} \tau(\lambda_g^* x) \Phi^{-1}(\delta_g) = \sum_{g\in G} \tau(\lambda_g^* x) \Phi^{-1} (\lambda_g \delta_e) = \sum_{g\in G} \tau(\lambda_g^* x) \widehat{\lambda_g}
   \end{align*}
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- lem-12: body_md -->
\label{lem:mult_is_convolution}
Let $G$ be a countable discrete group. Then for all $x \in L(G)$, we have $\widehat{x} \in \ell^2(G)$. Moreover, $\ell^1(G) \subseteq \widehat{L(G)} \subseteq \ell^2(G)$. Consequently, for all $x, y \in L(G)$ and for every $g \in G$, the convolution sum defining $(\widehat{x} \ast \widehat{y})(g)$ converges absolutely, and we have
$$\widehat{x} * \widehat{y} = \widehat{xy}.$$
In particular, $\widehat{x} \ast \widehat{y} \in \ell^2(G)$.
<!-- end lem-12 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
From Lemma \ref{lem:fourier_coeff}-(ii) we get that $\widehat{x}(g) = \langle \eta(x), \eta(\lambda_g)\rangle_{L^2}$. Thus 
    \[
    \sum_g |\widehat{x}(g)|^2 = \|\eta(x)\|_\tau^2 <\infty.
    \]
     The convolution of $\widehat{x}$ and $\widehat{y}$ at $g \in G$ is defined as
     $$(\widehat{x} * \widehat{y})(g) = \sum_{h \in G} \widehat{x}(h) \widehat{y}(h^{-1}g).$$
    By Cauchy-Schwartz inequality, this convolution sum converges absolutely, i.e., $(\widehat{x} * \widehat{y})(g)$ exists for all $g \in G$. 
    
    Now for any $x,y \in L(G)$ and $g\in G$, we have 

    \begin{align*}
        \widehat{xy}(g) = \langle \eta(xy), \eta(\lambda_g)\rangle_{L^2}= \langle xy \delta_e, \delta_g \rangle_{\ell^2}
    &=\langle y \delta_e, x^*\delta_g\rangle_{\ell^2}\\
    &= \sum_{h \in G} \langle y \delta_e, \delta_h \rangle_{\ell^2} \langle  \delta_h, x^*\delta_g \rangle_{\ell^2}\\
    &= \sum_h \widehat{y}(h) \langle \lambda_g^* x \lambda_h \delta_e, \delta_e \rangle =\sum_h \widehat{y}(h)\widehat{x}(gh^{-1})=(\widehat{x} \ast \widehat{y})(g).
    \end{align*}

This completes the proof!
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- prop-10: body_md -->
\label{prop:fourier-facts}
    Let $G$ be a countable discrete group. Then the following statements hold:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item[(i)] $\widehat{L(G)}$ is an involutive algebra with respect to the convolution product, where the involution $\xi^*$ of $\xi:G\to\mathbb{C}$ is defined by
        \[
